newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Sudan said bombing civilians, ousts U.N. envoy.
newsitem.headline: Sudan said bombing civilians, ousts U.N. envoy.

text.p: A United Nations envoy and a Christian group said on Friday Sudanese forces were destroying villages in the south-east of the country where the government is facing a mounting challenge from rebels.

In a statement and an urgent appeal to top U.N. humanitarian officials, the Swiss-based Christian Solidarity International (CSI) said Sudan had launched a "scorched earth" policy which had left some 50,000 people in the verge of starvation.

And at an unrelated news conference, Gaspar Biro, a special investigator for the world body's Human Rights Commission, said he believed Khartoum had been working for some time "to keep the population on the move" to deprive insurgents of a base.

Biro, a 39-year-old Hungarian law professor, said he had been compelled to leave Sudan soon after arrival this week when the country's prosecutor-general Abdul-Rahman Ibrahim told him his security could not be guaranteed.

The investigator, barred from Sudan for three years until last summer after issuing critical reports of its rights record, said Ibrahim asserted that he had been named at an official anti-rebel rally in Khartoum earlier in the day as part of "an international conspiracy" against the country.
"I felt I had no choice but to leave," said Biro, who had planned a week-long stay as part of preparations for his next report to be submitted to the Commission in March.

In its statement, CSI said a two-member team it send on a covert visit last week to the south of Sudan's Blue Nile region reported that government forces were "bombing and torching" villages right across the area.
"The government is waging a new scorched earth policy against its own civilians in the closed areas of east-central Sudan near the Ethiopian border," added CSI, which has its headquarters in Zurich.
"Since the village-razing programme was launched last spring, at least 50,000 people have been forced to flee from their homes," the statement declared.
Most of the displaced -- who CSI said included Moslems as well as Christians and animists -- were living in makeshift shelters or in the open, reduced to scavenging for food.

"Many are now dying of starvation and disease," the statement said, citing the team -- British parliamentarian Baroness Caroline Cox and CSI official John Eibner, who have both made previous undercover visits to Sudan.

In a letter to U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees Sadako Ogata and High Commissioner for Human Rights Jose Ayala Lasso, CSI appealed for urgent emergency airdrops of food and medicines to the displaced.
Failure by the international community to launch a quick relief "will condemn thousands to death by starvation and disease," the letter said.
CSI said villages were being destroyed by aerial bombardment with Antonov bombers and helicopter gunships combined with ground attacks by the army and government-supported militias.

Khartoum policy, CSI declared, appeared intended to punish the local population for supporting the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) -- which earlier on Friday said it had captured the town of Maban in the Blue Nile region.

The area has long been closed to U.N. and other international relief agencies. CSI said Eibner and Baroness Cox, a member of the British House of Lords, had delivered one tonne of emergency medical supplies to the refugees.

"But much more is needed to sustain the destitute displaced population in their own land and to avert a major humanitarian crisis in neighbouring Ethiopia" to where several thousand had fled, the statement added.
